children.summary: Computing is the systematic use of computers and algorithms to process information, turning raw inputs into useful outputs through a defined set of steps.

blocks.content: At its core, computing means using algorithms, step-by-step instructions, to take in data, process it, and produce a result. That's true whether you're running a formula in Excel, querying a database, or training a machine learning model. Every computing task, no matter how advanced, breaks down into this same input-process-output pattern.

blocks.title: Why This Matters for Analytics
items: Input: Raw data, transaction records, survey responses, sensor readings.
Process: The logic applied, a pivot table, a SQL query, a statistical model.
Output: Decision-ready information, a report, a dashboard, a forecast.

children.summary: Hardware is the physical machinery; software is the set of instructions that tells that machinery what to do. Analytics work needs both working together.

blocks.content: Hardware is the physical part of a computing system: processors, memory, storage, network devices. Software is the set of instructions, the programs, that run on that hardware to perform tasks. Neither one is useful on its own. Hardware provides the capacity to compute, while software directs what actually gets computed.

blocks.title: Hardware vs Software at a Glance

children.summary: The operating system is the software layer that manages a computer's hardware and lets every other program run. Windows, macOS, and Linux are the three you'll run into most.

blocks.content: Every piece of software you use, Excel, a browser, Python, runs on top of an operating system (OS). It manages memory, processing power, storage, and connected devices so applications don't have to deal with that complexity themselves.

blocks.title: The Three You'll Meet Most Often
items: Windows: The standard for most business desktops and corporate environments.
macOS: Common in creative and development-focused roles.
Linux: Rarely seen directly, but it's what most cloud servers and data infrastructure actually run on behind the scenes.

children.summary: GUIs let you interact with software visually, using clicks and menus. CLIs let you interact by typing commands. Analytics leans on both.

blocks.content: A Graphical User Interface (GUI) lets you interact with software visually, think Excel's ribbon menus or Power BI's drag-and-drop canvas. A Command Line Interface (CLI) means typing text commands instead, the way you'd run a Python script or a SQL query. GUIs are easier to pick up; CLIs scale and automate faster.

blocks.title: Where You'll See Each
items: GUI examples: Excel, Power BI, Tableau, point-and-click analytics tools.
CLI examples: Running a Python script, querying a database via SQL.
The trend: As you move from Excel toward Python and SQL in this course, you'll shift from GUI-first to CLI-comfortable work.

children.summary: Local systems run entirely on the device in front of you. Cloud systems run on someone else's servers and are reached over the internet. Most analytics tools today blend both.

blocks.content: A local system stores and processes data on your own machine. You get full control and no dependence on an internet connection. A cloud system stores and processes data on remote servers owned by a provider like Microsoft or Amazon, accessed over the internet, trading some control for accessibility, scalability, and easier collaboration.

blocks.title: Local vs Cloud
rows: From any device with internet access
Multiple people can work on the same file at once
A spreadsheet saved on your laptop
A file shared via OneDrive or Google Drive

children.summary: From the abacus to generative AI: how computing power evolved from room-sized machines into tools every business now runs on.
Computing moved from manual counting tools through mechanical, then electronic, then digital machines, with each stage making calculation faster and less dependent on human labour.

blocks.content: Long before electricity, people used physical tools like the abacus to track quantities and do arithmetic. Over centuries, mechanical calculators automated basic arithmetic. By the mid-20th century, electronic computers replaced moving parts with circuits, making calculation thousands of times faster. Each leap didn't just speed things up; it changed what kinds of problems businesses could realistically solve.

blocks.title: Key Milestones
items: Abacus (c. 2000 BCE): One of the earliest counting tools, still used in parts of the world today.
Mechanical calculators (1600s to 1800s): Devices like Pascal's calculator automated addition and subtraction using gears.
First electronic computers (1940s): Machines like ENIAC used vacuum tubes to calculate electronically, filling entire rooms.
Microprocessors (1970s): Shrinking a computer's core processing power onto a single chip made personal, affordable computers possible.

children.summary: Mainframes were large, centralized computers that businesses accessed through terminals, the first computers organizations used to run core operations like payroll and banking.

blocks.content: From the 1950s through the 1970s, computing meant one very large, very expensive machine housed in a dedicated room, shared by an entire organization. Employees didn't have their own computer. They connected to the mainframe through simple terminals that sent requests and displayed results. This era made computing core business infrastructure, even though only large organizations could afford it.

blocks.title: What Defined the Mainframe Era
items: Centralized model: One powerful machine served hundreds of users at once through terminals.
Batch processing: Jobs like a payroll run were submitted and processed in scheduled batches, not instantly.
High cost, high reliability: Usually only banks, insurers, airlines, and governments could justify the expense.
Business use cases: Payroll, accounting ledgers, inventory, early banking transaction systems.

children.summary: The personal computer moved processing power out of a shared central room and onto individual desks, and gave rise to the spreadsheet as a business tool.

blocks.content: Affordable personal computers arrived in the late 1970s and early 1980s, including the IBM PC in 1981, so employees no longer had to share time on one central machine. Software built for individual use, most notably early spreadsheet programs like VisiCalc and Lotus 1-2-3, put financial modelling and calculation directly into accountants' and managers' hands for the first time.

blocks.title: Why This Shift Mattered for Business
items: Decentralization: Computing power moved from a central IT room to individual desks across the organization.
Birth of the spreadsheet: Financial planning, budgeting, and forecasting became something an individual could do directly, without IT support.
Lower cost of entry: Small and mid-sized businesses could now afford computing power too, not just large corporations.

children.summary: Connecting computers into networks turned isolated desktop tools into a global, always-on infrastructure for communication and data exchange.

blocks.content: Through the 1990s, the internet connected previously isolated computers into a single global network. Email replaced much business correspondence, the web made information instantly accessible, and e-commerce opened entirely new ways for businesses to reach customers. For the first time, data and documents could move between organizations in seconds instead of days.

blocks.title: Business Impact
items: Real-time communication: Email and instant messaging replaced much postal and fax correspondence.
Online transactions: E-commerce opened direct-to-customer sales channels with no physical storefront needed.
Global reach: A business could serve customers and coordinate suppliers anywhere in the world.

children.summary: Cloud computing lets businesses rent computing power and storage over the internet instead of owning and maintaining physical servers.

blocks.content: Instead of buying and maintaining physical servers on-site, cloud computing lets an organization rent computing power, storage, and software over the internet from providers like Amazon, Microsoft, or Google, paying only for what it uses. That shifted IT spending from a large upfront capital cost to a flexible, ongoing operating expense, and let even small businesses scale their computing needs up or down instantly.

blocks.title: On-Premises vs Cloud
rows: High: buy servers and hardware outright
Managed by the organization's own IT team

children.summary: Computers have moved from following fixed, pre-written instructions to learning patterns from data, the shift behind today's forecasting tools, chatbots, and recommendation engines.

blocks.content: Traditional software follows rules a programmer writes explicitly: if this happens, do that. Artificial Intelligence, and the machine learning techniques behind most of it, instead learns patterns directly from historical data and uses those patterns to make predictions or decisions on new data. The recent acceleration in AI comes from two things arriving at once: far larger datasets to learn from, and far cheaper computing power, often cloud-based, to process them.

blocks.title: Where AI Shows Up in Business Today
items: Fraud detection: Flagging unusual transaction patterns in real time.
Demand forecasting: Predicting future sales or inventory needs from historical data.
Chatbots and virtual assistants: Handling routine customer queries automatically.
Generative AI tools: Drafting reports, summarizing documents, and writing code or formulas, covered later in this course.

children.summary: Four fast-moving technology areas reshaping how businesses collect data, secure transactions, and compute. Worth understanding even if you'll never build them yourself.
The Internet of Things connects everyday physical objects, sensors, machines, vehicles, to the internet, so they continuously generate data businesses can analyze.

blocks.content: The Internet of Things (IoT) covers physical devices, from warehouse sensors to delivery vehicles to wearable fitness trackers, that connect to the internet and continuously collect and transmit data. Earlier eras of computing relied on people manually entering data. IoT devices generate it automatically and constantly, often in far greater volume than any team could capture by hand.

blocks.title: Business Examples
items: Inventory sensors: Automatically tracking stock levels in a warehouse in real time.
Fleet tracking: GPS and sensor data monitoring delivery vehicle location, fuel use, and condition.
Wearable devices: Feeding data into corporate wellness or safety monitoring programs.

children.summary: Blockchain is a shared, tamper-resistant digital ledger that lets multiple parties trust the same record of a transaction without needing a central authority.

blocks.content: A blockchain is a digital record-keeping system shared across many computers, where each new entry is cryptographically linked to the one before it, making past records extremely hard to alter without detection. That matters for business because it lets organizations that don't fully trust each other, suppliers, banks, auditors, agree on a shared version of events without any single party controlling the record.

blocks.title: Business Relevance
items: Supply chain traceability: Recording each step a product takes from raw material to shelf.
Cross-border payments: Settling transactions between parties in different countries without relying on multiple intermediary banks.
Audit trails: Creating records that are hard to quietly alter after the fact, relevant to internal controls and assurance.

children.summary: Generative AI systems create new content, text, images, code, rather than only analyzing existing data, changing how analysts draft reports and explore information.

blocks.content: Most earlier AI systems were built to analyze or classify existing data, for example flagging a transaction as likely fraudulent. Generative AI is different. It produces new content, writing text, generating images, writing code, based on patterns learned from vast amounts of existing material. Tools built on this technology, including large language models, are increasingly used directly inside everyday business software.

blocks.title: Emerging Use Cases
items: Drafting first versions: Reports, emails, and summaries that a human then reviews and refines.
Summarizing data: Turning a large dataset or document into a short, readable overview.
Writing code and formulas: Generating a starting SQL query, Excel formula, or Python script from a plain-language description.

children.summary: Quantum computing is an emerging approach that could eventually solve certain complex problems far faster than today's computers. Still early-stage, but worth being aware of.

blocks.content: Traditional computers process information as bits that are either 0 or 1. Quantum computers take a different physical approach that, in theory, lets them explore many possibilities at once, making them potentially far faster at specific problems such as complex optimization or breaking certain forms of encryption. The technology is still experimental and not yet part of everyday business computing, but it's worth knowing about given how it could eventually affect data security and complex forecasting.

blocks.title: Why It's on the Radar, Not Yet in Use
items: Still experimental: Current quantum computers are limited, expensive, and mostly confined to research labs.

Long-term security implications: A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could eventually break some of today's encryption methods, which is why governments and large firms are watching this space closely.
Potential future upside: Faster solutions to complex optimization problems, such as portfolio or logistics optimization.

children.summary: The core software and infrastructure categories that run a modern organization's operations, data, and finances.
Enterprise applications are large-scale software systems that run core business functions, finance, HR, supply chain, across an entire organization rather than for one individual.

blocks.content: Personal computing gave individuals their own tools. Enterprise applications go further, serving an entire organization at once and keeping data consistent across departments. Instead of separate spreadsheets for finance, HR, and inventory that quickly fall out of sync, an enterprise application keeps one shared version of the data that every department reads from and writes to.

blocks.title: Common Categories
items: ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning): Integrates finance, procurement, and operations, covered in the next topic.
CRM (Customer Relationship Management): Tracks customer interactions, sales pipelines, and service history.
HRIS (Human Resource Information System): Manages employee records, payroll, and benefits.

children.summary: ERP systems integrate finance, procurement, inventory, and HR into one connected system of record, replacing disconnected departmental spreadsheets.

blocks.content: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems are the backbone of most mid-to-large organizations' operations. Instead of finance, procurement, and inventory each keeping separate records, an ERP system ties these functions together, so a purchase order automatically updates inventory and flows through to the accounting ledger without anyone re-entering the same data twice.

blocks.title: Major ERP Platforms
rows: Large multinational enterprises with complex, global operations
Large enterprises, especially those needing deep financial management
Mid-sized businesses already using the Microsoft ecosystem

children.summary: Databases are the organized digital storage systems that hold nearly all of a business's transactional and operational data, from sales records to customer details.

blocks.content: A database is a structured system for storing, organizing, and retrieving data reliably, the foundation underneath almost every business application, including the ERP and CRM systems already covered. Instead of data sitting in scattered files, a database keeps it organized in tables so it can be searched, updated, and reported on consistently by many users at once. Module 8 (Database Systems) and Module 9 (SQL) come back to this topic in much greater depth.

blocks.title: What to Know at This Stage
items: Structured storage: Data is organized into tables of rows and columns, similar in shape to a spreadsheet but built to handle far larger volumes reliably.
Single source of truth: Every system that needs the data, finance, sales, operations, reads from the same underlying database.
Foundation for analytics: Nearly every report, dashboard, and analysis in this course ultimately traces back to data sitting in a database.

children.summary: Servers are the physical or virtual machines that run applications and store data behind the scenes, whether housed on-site or in a remote data center.

blocks.content: A server is simply a computer dedicated to providing a service to other computers, hosting a website, running a database, storing shared files. Businesses used to house their own servers on-site in a dedicated server room. Today, many of those same workloads run instead on servers inside a cloud provider's data center, accessed remotely over the internet.

blocks.title: Where Servers Live Today
items: On-premises: Physical servers owned and maintained in the organization's own building.
Data center hosting: Physical servers owned by a provider but dedicated to one organization's use.
Virtual servers (cloud): Software-defined servers running on shared cloud infrastructure, scaled up or down on demand.

children.summary: Cloud platforms are the major providers, AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, that rent out computing infrastructure so businesses don't have to own physical servers.

blocks.content: A small number of large providers now supply most of the world's cloud infrastructure, renting out computing power, storage, and pre-built services (including AI tools) that businesses would otherwise need to build and maintain themselves. Choosing a cloud platform is now a routine business decision, similar in weight to choosing an ERP vendor.

blocks.title: The Three Major Providers
items: Amazon Web Services (AWS): The largest provider by market share, widely used across industries.
Microsoft Azure: Popular with organizations already using Microsoft 365 and Windows-based systems.
Google Cloud Platform (GCP): Often chosen for its strength in data analytics and machine learning tools.

children.summary: The raw material of every analysis in this course: what data actually is, where it comes from, and the different forms it takes.
Data is any raw fact or observation, a number, a word, a date, that on its own doesn't tell you much, but becomes valuable once it's organized and analyzed.

blocks.content: On its own, the number "45,000" is just data. It means nothing until you know it's a sales figure, for which month, in which currency. Data is the raw, unprocessed starting point of every analysis; everything else in this course is about turning it into something useful.

blocks.title: Examples of Data in Business
items: A transaction amount recorded at the point of sale.
A customer's name and email address in a CRM system.
A timestamp recording when an invoice was issued.
A single click on a website page.

children.summary: Analytics has grown from simple manual bookkeeping and reporting into today's automated, AI-assisted analysis of massive datasets in real time.

blocks.content: Businesses have always used data to make decisions. Only the tools have changed. What once took a bookkeeper days with a paper ledger now happens automatically, continuously, at a scale no human team could match by hand.

blocks.title: The Broad Stages
items: Manual record-keeping: Paper ledgers and handwritten reports.
Spreadsheet era: Excel put calculation and modelling on every desk.
Business Intelligence: Dashboards and automated reporting across an organization.
Big Data and AI: Real-time analysis of massive, fast-moving datasets.

children.summary: Data moves through a predictable set of stages from the moment it's collected to the moment it's archived or deleted. Knowing this cycle helps you spot where quality issues creep in.

blocks.content: Almost every data quality problem you'll run into traces back to a weak point somewhere in this cycle, often at collection or cleaning, long before anyone runs an analysis.

blocks.title: Stages of the Data Life Cycle
items: Collection: Data is captured, a sale is recorded, a form is submitted.
Storage: Data is saved in a file, database, or system.
Processing and cleaning: Errors are fixed and data is reshaped for use.
Analysis: Patterns and answers are pulled from the data.
Reporting and sharing: Findings are communicated to decision-makers.
Archiving or deletion: Data is kept for records or removed once it's no longer needed.

children.summary: Data Engineering, Data Analysis, and Data Science are related but distinct disciplines, each focused on a different stage of turning raw data into value.

blocks.title: The Three Domains
rows: Building and maintaining reliable pipelines and infrastructure
Clean, accessible data ready for others to use
Interpreting existing data to answer business questions

children.summary: Big Data means datasets too large or fast-moving for traditional tools to handle. AI is one of the main technologies now used to make sense of it.

blocks.content: A dataset that would crash Excel or take days to process by hand falls into Big Data territory. AI and machine learning are closely tied to this shift, since these techniques need very large amounts of data to learn useful patterns from, and cheaper cloud computing has made storing and processing that much data affordable for the first time.

blocks.title: Where the Two Meet
items: Fraud detection systems scan millions of transactions for unusual patterns.
Recommendation engines learn from billions of past interactions.
Demand forecasting models are trained on years of historical sales data.

children.summary: Data becomes information once it's organized and given context, and becomes knowledge once it's understood well enough to guide a decision.

blocks.title: From Data to Knowledge
rows: Information understood well enough to act on
"March sales rose because of the new promotion, worth repeating in Q3"

children.summary: Structured data is organized into a fixed format of rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or database table, which makes it easy to search and analyze.

blocks.content: Structured data is the easiest type to work with, because every record follows the same predictable layout: the same columns, in the same order, for every row. Most of the analytics techniques in this course are built around structured data.

blocks.title: Examples
items: An Excel sales ledger with one row per transaction.
A customer database with fixed fields for name, email, and address.
An accounting general ledger.

children.summary: Semi-structured data has some organizational structure but doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns, think emails or JSON files.

blocks.content: Semi-structured data sits between fully organized spreadsheets and completely free-form text. It has identifiable elements, like a sender and subject line in an email, but the overall shape can vary from one record to the next.

blocks.title: Examples
items: An email, with a defined sender, subject, and body, but free-form content.
A JSON or XML file exchanged automatically between two business systems.
An invoice where the number of line items varies from one document to the next.

children.summary: Unstructured data has no predefined organization at all, which makes it the hardest type to search and analyze directly. Think free text, images, and audio.

blocks.content: Unstructured data makes up most of the data generated worldwide, but it can't just be dropped into a spreadsheet the way structured data can. Making sense of it usually takes more advanced tools, including AI, to extract structure from it first.

blocks.title: Examples
items: Customer reviews or open-text survey responses.
Call centre recordings.
Social media posts.
A scanned PDF contract.

children.summary: What data analytics actually means in practice, why organizations invest in it, and how it fits into everyday accounting and finance decisions.
Data analytics is the process of examining data to find patterns, answer questions, and support decisions: turning numbers into direction.

blocks.content: At its simplest, data analytics means asking a question, then using data to answer it, whether that's "which product sold best last quarter?" or "which customers are most likely to churn?" The techniques range from a simple Excel filter to a machine learning model, but the underlying goal never changes.

blocks.title: What the Process Involves
items: Collecting relevant data.
Cleaning and preparing it.
Analyzing it to find patterns or answers.
Visualizing and communicating the findings.

children.summary: Organizations that use data to guide decisions tend to consistently outperform those relying on gut feeling alone, because analytics cuts guesswork and surfaces patterns people would otherwise miss.

blocks.title: What Good Analytics Delivers
items: Faster problem detection: Spotting a revenue dip or cost overrun before it becomes serious.
More accurate forecasting: Basing plans on historical patterns, not assumptions.
Evidence-based decisions: Backing choices with data rather than opinion.
Competitive advantage: Reacting to market shifts faster than competitors relying on intuition alone.

children.summary: Data-driven decision making means basing choices on evidence from data rather than intuition alone, though good judgement still matters in interpreting what the data shows.

blocks.content: Being data-driven doesn't mean removing human judgement. It means using data as the starting point for a decision, and judgement to work out what that data actually means for the business.

blocks.title: What It Looks Like in Practice
items: Setting measurable KPIs before launching an initiative.
Testing a decision on a small scale before rolling it out widely.
Reviewing outcomes against the original data afterward, not just moving on.

children.summary: Accounting and finance were among the earliest business functions to use data intensively, and analytics now extends that tradition, from variance analysis to fraud detection.

blocks.title: Where Analytics Already Lives in Your Field
items: Variance analysis: Comparing budget to actual figures to explain differences.
Cash flow forecasting: Predicting future cash positions from historical patterns.
Fraud and anomaly detection: Flagging transactions that don't fit expected patterns.
Automated reconciliation: Matching records across systems without manual checking.

children.summary: Data used in analytics comes from many places inside and outside an organization: internal systems, external providers, and increasingly, direct user input.

blocks.title: Types of Data Sources
items: Internal systems: ERP, accounting, and CRM software already used daily.
External sources: Market data providers, government statistics, industry reports.
Primary collection: Surveys, forms, and interviews you design yourself.
Automated sources: Sensors, APIs, and website activity logs.

children.summary: A structured process analysts follow from defining a business question through to delivering an answer, keeping analysis focused rather than open-ended exploration.

blocks.title: The Lifecycle
items: 1. Define the question: What business decision does this analysis need to support?
2. Collect relevant data: Gather only what's needed to answer it.
3. Clean and prepare: Fix errors and reshape data for analysis.
4. Analyze and model: Apply the right technique to find the answer.
5. Communicate findings: Share results clearly with the people who need to act on them.
6. Monitor outcomes: Check whether the decision produced the expected result.

children.summary: Four questions analytics can answer, what happened, why it happened, what will happen, and what should be done, each needing a different technique.
Descriptive analytics summarizes what has already happened, the starting point for almost every business report, from monthly sales totals to KPI dashboards.

blocks.content: Descriptive analytics answers "what happened?" by summarizing historical data. It's the simplest and most common type of analysis, and usually the first step before anything more advanced.

blocks.title: Examples
items: A monthly sales report showing total revenue by product.
A headcount summary by department.
A website traffic report for the past quarter.

children.summary: Diagnostic analytics digs into why something happened, usually by comparing data across time periods, segments, or against a budget or benchmark.

blocks.content: Diagnostic analytics answers "why did this happen?" It goes a step beyond description, comparing, segmenting, and drilling into data to find the cause behind a result.

blocks.title: Examples
items: A variance analysis explaining why costs rose above budget.
A drill-down analysis identifying which region drove a sales decline.

children.summary: Predictive analytics uses historical data and statistical models to estimate what's likely to happen next, such as forecasting next quarter's revenue.

blocks.content: Predictive analytics answers "what's likely to happen next?" by finding patterns in historical data and projecting them forward. It doesn't guarantee an outcome. It estimates a probability based on what's happened before.

blocks.title: Examples
items: Forecasting next quarter's cash flow from historical trends.
Predicting product demand ahead of a busy season.
Scoring a customer's credit risk.

children.summary: Prescriptive analytics goes a step further than prediction by recommending a specific course of action, the most advanced and least commonly implemented of the four types.

blocks.content: Prescriptive analytics answers "what should we do about it?" It combines prediction with optimization to recommend a specific action, not just a forecast. It's the most complex type of analytics, and the one you'll see least often as a beginner.

blocks.title: Examples
items: Recommending exactly how much stock to reorder and when.
Suggesting an optimal price point to maximize revenue.
Optimizing delivery routes to minimize cost.

children.summary: The job titles you'll run into across the data and analytics profession, and how they typically divide the work.
Data Engineers build and maintain the pipelines and infrastructure that move data from its source into a usable, reliable form for others to analyze.

blocks.content: Data Engineers rarely analyze data themselves. Instead, they build the plumbing that gets clean, reliable data flowing from source systems into the databases and warehouses that analysts and scientists depend on.

children.summary: Data Analysts interpret existing data to answer specific business questions, typically producing reports, dashboards, and recommendations.

blocks.content: This is the role closest to the day-to-day work in this course: taking data that already exists, analyzing it, and turning the findings into a report or dashboard a manager can act on.

children.summary: Data Scientists build predictive models and algorithms, often using statistics and machine learning to answer more open-ended, forward-looking questions.

blocks.content: Where a Data Analyst typically explains what has already happened, a Data Scientist more often builds models that predict what happens next, using statistical and machine learning techniques.

children.summary: Business Analysts bridge business needs and technical solutions, translating a business problem into requirements a data or IT team can act on.

blocks.content: A Business Analyst focuses less on the technical analysis itself and more on understanding what the business actually needs, then turning that into clear requirements for a technical team to build.

children.summary: Financial Analysts apply analytical techniques specifically to financial data, budgeting, forecasting, valuation, to support financial decision-making.

blocks.content: A Financial Analyst applies the same broad analytical thinking as a Data Analyst, but specialized in financial data: building budgets, forecasts, and valuations to support investment and business decisions.

children.summary: AI Engineers design, build, and deploy AI and machine learning systems into real products and workflows, an increasingly common role as generative AI adoption grows.

blocks.content: AI Engineers take AI and machine learning models, often built by data scientists, and integrate them into real, working products and systems that other people or systems can use directly.

children.summary: The building blocks of Excel, structured tables and formulas, that turn a grid of numbers into a working calculation engine.

blocks.content: Before any advanced analysis, Excel work starts with two fundamentals: organizing data into proper tables, and writing formulas that calculate automatically whenever the underlying data changes.

blocks.title: Key Building Blocks
items: Tables: Structured, sortable ranges that expand automatically as you add data.
Formulas: Calculations that update instantly when inputs change.
Cell referencing: Relative references shift when copied; absolute references ($A$1) stay fixed.

children.summary: Excel's core analytical formulas: lookups to pull matching data, logic functions to test conditions, and date functions to work with time periods.
Pivot Tables let you summarize thousands of rows into a compact, reorganizable report in a few clicks, without writing a single formula.

blocks.content: A Pivot Table takes a large, detailed dataset and lets you summarize it by any category you choose, total sales by region, headcount by department, just by dragging fields into place instead of writing formulas.

blocks.title: Why Analysts Rely on Them
items: Aggregate thousands of rows into a compact summary instantly.
Reshape the view by dragging fields, without touching the underlying data.
Answer "how much / how many by category" questions faster than any other Excel tool.

children.summary: Turning summarized data into charts and dashboards that communicate a finding at a glance, instead of making the reader parse a table of numbers.

blocks.content: A well-chosen chart lets a reader grasp a finding in seconds. A table of the same numbers forces them to do the work themselves. The right chart type depends entirely on the question you're answering.

blocks.title: Choosing a Chart Type
items: Bar chart: Comparing values across categories.
Line chart: Showing a trend over time.
Pie chart: Showing parts of a whole. Use sparingly, and only with few categories.

children.summary: Data can be collected in several ways, from manual entry to fully automated feeds. The right method depends on volume, frequency, and source.

blocks.title: Collection Methods
rows: Data typed in directly by a person
Automated data feeds from another system
Public data with no API available

children.summary: Good analysis is only possible with good data. Quality is typically judged across accuracy, completeness, and validity.

blocks.title: Dimensions of Data Quality
rows: Does it follow the expected format and rules?

children.summary: Before analysis can begin, raw data almost always needs cleaning: handling missing values, unusual outliers, and duplicate records.

blocks.title: Common Cleaning Tasks
items: Missing values: Decide whether to fill, estimate, or exclude them. Never ignore them silently.
Outliers: Investigate before removing. An unusual value could be genuine, not an error.
Duplicates: Remove to avoid double-counting in totals and averages.

children.summary: Transformation reshapes and enhances raw data into a form ready for analysis, standardizing formats and adding useful new information.

blocks.title: What Transformation Covers
items: Formatting: Standardizing dates, currencies, and units of measurement.
Enrichment: Adding calculated fields, or joining in useful external reference data.

children.summary: Programming lets you automate repetitive tasks and scale analysis beyond what's practical by hand or even in a spreadsheet.

blocks.title: Why Analysts Learn to Code
items: Automate reporting tasks that would otherwise be repeated manually every month.
Handle datasets too large for Excel to process comfortably.
Repeat an analysis reliably, exactly the same way, every single time.

children.summary: The basic vocabulary every programming language shares: variables to store values, data types to define what kind of value it is, and operators to work with them.

blocks.title: Core Vocabulary
rows: A named container for a value
What kind of value it holds
A symbol that performs an action

children.summary: Control flow determines the order code runs in. Conditions decide which path to take, and loops repeat an action automatically.

blocks.title: Two Core Patterns
items: If/else conditions: Run different code depending on whether a condition is true or false.
Loops: Repeat the same action across every row of a dataset, instead of writing it out by hand.

children.summary: A function is a reusable, named block of code that takes inputs (parameters) and produces an output (return value). Write it once, use it many times.

blocks.content: A function packages up a piece of logic so it can be reused without rewriting it. It typically takes one or more inputs (parameters), does something with them, and hands back a result (a return value), much like an Excel formula takes inputs and returns a calculated result.

children.summary: Object-oriented programming organizes code around 'objects' that bundle data and behaviour together, built from reusable templates called classes.

blocks.content: A class is a template describing a type of thing, say, a "Customer", including the data it holds (name, balance) and the actions it can perform (place an order). An object is one specific instance built from that template. You won't need to write object-oriented code early on, but you'll recognize the pattern in most real-world Python libraries.

children.summary: Programming languages are either compiled, translated into machine code ahead of time, or interpreted, translated and run line by line. Python, which you'll learn next, is interpreted.

blocks.title: Compiled vs Interpreted
rows: Fully translated into machine code before running
Translated and run line-by-line as it executes

children.summary: The core Python skills needed before any data-specific work: syntax, data structures, functions, and handling errors.
Before writing any Python, you need somewhere to write and run it. Options range from simple to full-featured setups.

blocks.title: Common Options
items: Jupyter Notebook: Interactive, ideal for exploratory data analysis.
VS Code: A full-featured code editor for larger projects.
Google Colab: Runs entirely in the browser, no installation needed, great for getting started.

blocks.content: Throughout this module, we'll build up a small analysis for a fictional Colombo retail chain called Ceylon Mart. You'll use the same dataset across every topic, so set up whichever environment you're comfortable with now.

# Try This
# Open Jupyter Notebook, VS Code, or Google Colab and run this line.
# If you see the message printed below, your environment is ready.

print("Ceylon Mart analytics environment is ready.")

# Answer / Expected Output:
# Ceylon Mart analytics environment is ready.

children.summary: The basic grammar of Python: how to write valid code, store values in variables, perform operations, and get input or output.

blocks.content: Python's syntax reads almost like plain English. You'll store values in variables, use operators to calculate and compare, and use built-in functions like print() to display output, the same core building blocks covered in Module 5, now written as actual Python code.

# Try This
# Ceylon Mart's Colombo branch had these figures today.
# Store them in variables, then print a one-line summary.

branch_name = "Colombo"
daily_sales = 125000
is_open = True

# Write one print() statement combining all three variables.


# --- Answer ---
print(f"{branch_name} branch | Sales: Rs. {daily_sales} | Open: {is_open}")

# Expected Output:
# Colombo branch | Sales: Rs. 125000 | Open: True

children.summary: Python's core ways of holding multiple values at once. Each structure suits a different kind of data organization.

blocks.title: Python's Core Data Structures
rows: Key-value pairs, like a customer record
A collection of unique values only

blocks.content:
# Try This
# Ceylon Mart recorded these daily sales (in Rs. '000) for one week,
# and one customer's record as a dictionary.

daily_sales = [120, 135, 98, 150, 175, 210, 90]
customer = {"name": "N. Perera", "city": "Colombo", "loyalty_points": 340}

# 1. Find the total sales for the week.
# 2. Print the customer's city.


# --- Answer ---
total_sales = sum(daily_sales)
print("Weekly total (Rs. '000):", total_sales)
print("Customer city:", customer["city"])

# Expected Output:
# Weekly total (Rs. '000): 978
# Customer city: Colombo

children.summary: How Python code is organized and reused: from a single function, to a file of functions (a module), to a full toolkit others have built (a package or library).

blocks.content: Rather than writing everything from scratch, Python lets you reuse code at increasing scale: a function does one specific job; a module is a file grouping related functions together; a package or library is a full, published toolkit, like Pandas, that you install and import into your own work.

# Try This
# Write a function that calculates the total value of one Ceylon Mart
# order line, given a quantity and a unit price.

def calculate_line_total(quantity, unit_price):
    # your code here
    pass

# Test it on: 4 units at Rs. 350 each, and 12 units at Rs. 85 each.


# --- Answer ---
def calculate_line_total(quantity, unit_price):
    return quantity * unit_price

print(calculate_line_total(4, 350))
print(calculate_line_total(12, 85))

# Expected Output:
# 1400
# 1020

children.summary: Reading and writing the file formats analysts work with most often, CSV, Excel, and JSON, directly from Python code.

blocks.content: Almost every analysis starts by loading data from a file and ends by saving results back out. Python can read and write CSV files, Excel workbooks, and JSON files directly, which fits naturally into a workflow that already involves spreadsheets or other business systems.

# Try This
# Ceylon Mart keeps its daily orders in "ceylonmart_orders.csv" with
# columns: order_id, customer_name, city, product, quantity, unit_price.
# Read the file and print the first 3 rows.

import csv

# your code here


# --- Answer ---
import csv

with open("ceylonmart_orders.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    rows = list(reader)

for row in rows[:3]:
    print(row)

# Expected Output (example):
# {'order_id': '1001', 'customer_name': 'N. Perera', 'city': 'Colombo', 'product': 'Rice 5kg', 'quantity': '2', 'unit_price': '950'}
# ...and two more rows in the same shape.

children.summary: How to anticipate and gracefully handle things going wrong in code, and how to systematically find and fix bugs when they do.

blocks.content: Code will eventually run into something it doesn't expect, a missing file, a value in the wrong format. Error handling lets you plan for that and respond gracefully instead of letting the whole script crash. Debugging is the skill of reading an error message, isolating where the problem happened, and fixing it.

# Try This
# Ceylon Mart wants average order value: total sales divided by
# number of orders. Handle the case where there are zero orders.

def average_order_value(total_sales, order_count):
    # your code here
    pass

print(average_order_value(50000, 20))
print(average_order_value(0, 0))


# --- Answer ---
def average_order_value(total_sales, order_count):
    try:
        return total_sales / order_count
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        return 0

print(average_order_value(50000, 20))
print(average_order_value(0, 0))

# Expected Output:
# 2500.0
# 0

children.summary: Applying Python specifically to data analysis, using the libraries and workflows analysts rely on daily.
NumPy and Pandas are the two foundational Python libraries for data analysis. NumPy handles numerical computation, Pandas handles tabular data.

blocks.title: The Two Foundational Libraries
rows: Fast numerical operations on large arrays of numbers
Spreadsheet-like tables called DataFrames, the core tool for real-world data analysis in Python

blocks.content:
# Try This
# Load ceylonmart_orders.csv into a Pandas DataFrame and inspect it.

import pandas as pd

# your code here


# --- Answer ---
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("ceylonmart_orders.csv")
print(df.head())
