children.summary: Reshaping and combining datasets in Pandas: filtering rows to a subset, and merging separate tables together, similar to an Excel VLOOKUP but far more powerful.

blocks.content: Filtering narrows a dataset down to just the rows you need, for example only transactions above a certain amount. Merging combines two separate tables based on a shared key, similar in spirit to an Excel VLOOKUP, but able to join entire tables at once rather than one cell at a time.

# Try This
# From ceylonmart_orders.csv, filter to orders from "Colombo" only.
# Then merge in a loyalty_tier from a separate customers DataFrame.

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.read_csv("ceylonmart_orders.csv")
customers = pd.read_csv("ceylonmart_customers.csv")  # columns: customer_name, loyalty_tier

# your code here


# --- Answer ---
colombo_orders = orders[orders["city"] == "Colombo"]
merged = colombo_orders.merge(customers, on="customer_name", how="left")
print(merged.head())

# Expected Output:
# The Colombo orders, now with an extra loyalty_tier column attached.

children.summary: The first step of any real analysis: getting to know a dataset's shape, contents, and quirks before drawing conclusions from it.

blocks.title: A Typical EDA Checklist
items: Check the size of the dataset and what each column represents.
Look for missing or unexpected values.
Review summary statistics: averages, ranges, counts.
Spot obvious outliers before they distort later analysis.

blocks.content:
# Try This
# Run a quick EDA pass on ceylonmart_orders.csv.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("ceylonmart_orders.csv")

# 1. Check for missing values in every column.
# 2. Get summary statistics for the quantity column.
# 3. Count how many orders came from each city.


# --- Answer ---
print(df.isnull().sum())
print(df["quantity"].describe())
print(df["city"].value_counts())

# Expected Output:
# A column-by-column count of missing values (ideally all zero),
# summary stats for quantity (count, mean, min, max, etc.),
# and a count of orders per city, largest first.

children.summary: Python's two most common charting libraries. Matplotlib gives full control, Seaborn gives quicker, better-looking statistical charts.

blocks.content: Matplotlib is Python's foundational plotting library, with fine control over every element of a chart. Seaborn builds on top of it and is tuned for statistical charts, producing polished results with far less code. Most analysts default to Seaborn for everyday charts and drop into Matplotlib when they need finer control.

# Try This
# Plot Ceylon Mart's total sales by product category as a bar chart.

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("ceylonmart_orders.csv")
df["line_total"] = df["quantity"] * df["unit_price"]

# your code here


# --- Answer ---
category_sales = df.groupby("category")["line_total"].sum().reset_index()
sns.barplot(data=category_sales, x="category", y="line_total")
plt.title("Ceylon Mart: Sales by Category")
plt.show()

# Expected Output:
# A bar chart with one bar per product category, height showing total sales.

children.summary: Using Python to automate repetitive file-based work, such as processing every file in a folder without opening each one manually.

blocks.content: A recurring reporting task, opening twelve monthly files, pulling the same figures out of each, combining them, can be written once as a Python script and run automatically, saving hours of repetitive manual work every reporting cycle.

# Try This
# Ceylon Mart stores one CSV per month in a folder called "monthly_orders/".
# Combine all of them into a single DataFrame.

import pandas as pd
import glob

# your code here


# --- Answer ---
files = glob.glob("monthly_orders/*.csv")
all_orders = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in files], ignore_index=True)
print(all_orders.shape)

# Expected Output:
# The combined row and column count across every monthly file,
# for example (2880, 6) if there are 12 months of 240 rows each.

children.summary: Bringing Python skills together to solve real accounting and finance problems, the payoff for everything learned in this module.

blocks.title: Practical Examples
items: Automating bank reconciliation between a statement and the general ledger.
Consolidating monthly reports from dozens of separate Excel files into one.
Flagging unusual or potentially fraudulent transactions for manual review.

blocks.content:
# Try This
# Ceylon Mart's accountant wants to reconcile the bank statement against
# the internal sales ledger. Flag any order amount that doesn't appear
# in the bank statement at all.

import pandas as pd

ledger = pd.read_csv("ceylonmart_orders.csv")
ledger["line_total"] = ledger["quantity"] * ledger["unit_price"]
bank_statement = pd.read_csv("ceylonmart_bank_statement.csv")  # column: amount

# your code here


# --- Answer ---
unmatched = ledger[~ledger["line_total"].isin(bank_statement["amount"])]
print("Orders with no matching bank entry:")
print(unmatched[["order_id", "line_total"]])

# Expected Output:
# A short list of order IDs and amounts that couldn't be matched
# to a bank transaction, worth a manual look.

children.summary: A database is an organized collection of data, structured so it can be easily accessed, managed, and updated.

blocks.content: Behind almost every business system, your ERP, your bank's app, an e-commerce site, sits a database, quietly storing and organizing the data that system depends on. Understanding databases is what makes SQL, covered next, make sense.

blocks.title: Database Objects
items: Table: Basic unit of storage; composed of rows and columns.
Primary key: A unique identifier for each row in a table.
Foreign key: A field linking to a row in another table, connecting related data without duplicating it.
View: Logically represents subsets of data from one or more tables.
Indexes: Improves the performance of some queries.
Users: It establishes authentication (who you are, usually via a password) and authorization (what you are allowed to do via privileges).
Schema: A logical container or namespace inside a database used to group related objects (like tables, views, and indexes).

children.summary: Relational databases store data in linked tables, connected through keys, so information isn't duplicated across the system.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
items: Table: A grid of rows and columns holding one type of data, like Customers or Orders.
View: A virtual table based on a SQL query that shows data from one or more base tables without storing its own copy.
Schema: A logical container or namespace inside a database used to group related objects, like tables, views, and indexes.
Users: Establish authentication (who you are, usually via a password) and authorization (what you're allowed to do, via privileges).
Keys: Fields that uniquely identify each row (primary keys) or link to a row in another table (foreign keys).
Sequence: A database object that automatically generates a sequential series of numbers, often used to assign unique ID values.
Index: A structure that speeds up data retrieval by letting the database find rows without scanning the entire table.

children.summary: SQL, the language used to work with databases, splits into subsets depending on the task: querying data, defining structure, or modifying records.
Database design principles that reduce duplicate data and keep information consistent, mainly through a process called normalization.

blocks.content: Normalization is the process of organizing a database's tables so each piece of data is stored in exactly one place. Done well, updating a customer's address once updates it everywhere that customer is referenced, instead of requiring the same edit across dozens of duplicated records.

children.summary: The broader infrastructure that supports databases in a business setting: servers, backups, and security layers working together.

blocks.content: A database doesn't run in isolation. It depends on servers to host it, backup systems to protect against data loss, and security controls to make sure only authorized people can access or change it.

children.summary: Cloud data warehouses are modern platforms built to store and analyze massive volumes of data, replacing traditional on-premises databases for many analytics workloads.

blocks.title: Examples
items: Snowflake: A widely used cloud data warehouse built for analytics at scale.
Google BigQuery: Google's serverless data warehouse, priced by usage.
Amazon Redshift: AWS's data warehouse, tightly integrated with the rest of AWS.

children.summary: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for asking questions of a database. Learning its basic rules is the first step to querying data directly.

blocks.content: SQL is the near-universal language for working with relational databases. Almost every database system, from a small business tool to an enterprise data warehouse, understands it. Its syntax reads close to plain English, which makes it one of the more approachable technical skills in this course.
Every SQL exercise in this module uses the same small database for Ceylon Mart, so you can build on what you've already written as you go.

-- Try This
-- Write a query that returns every column and every row from Customers.


-- Answer
SELECT * FROM Customers;

children.summary: The core building blocks of every SQL query: selecting which columns you want, filtering which rows, and controlling the order of results.

blocks.title: Core Keywords
rows: Remove duplicate rows from the results

blocks.content:
-- Try This
-- 1. List all customers from "Colombo", sorted by join_date (newest first).
-- 2. List the distinct cities Ceylon Mart has customers in.


-- Answer
SELECT customer_name, join_date
FROM Customers
WHERE city = 'Colombo'
ORDER BY join_date DESC;

SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM Customers;

children.summary: Operators that let you build precise filtering conditions in SQL, from simple comparisons to combining multiple conditions together.

blocks.title: Building Filter Conditions
items: Comparison operators: =, >, <, <> to compare values.
Logical operators: AND, OR, NOT to combine multiple conditions.
Pattern matching: LIKE, for partial text matches.

blocks.content:
-- Try This
-- Find products in the "Beverages" category priced above Rs. 500.


-- Answer
SELECT product_name, unit_price
FROM Products
WHERE category = 'Beverages'
  AND unit_price > 500;

children.summary: Aggregation functions collapse many rows into a single summary value, the SQL equivalent of an Excel pivot table calculation.

blocks.title: Common Aggregation Functions
rows: The total of a numeric column

blocks.content:
-- Try This
-- Find the total quantity sold and the average quantity per order line,
-- across all of OrderItems.


-- Answer
SELECT
    SUM(quantity) AS total_quantity_sold,
    AVG(quantity) AS avg_quantity_per_line
FROM OrderItems;

children.summary: GROUP BY splits data into categories before aggregating, and HAVING filters those grouped results. Together they answer 'how much, by category' questions.

blocks.content: GROUP BY is what turns a simple total into a breakdown, for example splitting total sales by region instead of returning one company-wide number. HAVING then lets you filter those grouped results, such as keeping only regions where sales exceeded a certain amount.

-- Try This
-- Find total quantity sold per product, but only show products where
-- total quantity sold exceeds 100 units.


-- Answer
SELECT
    product_id,
    SUM(quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM OrderItems
GROUP BY product_id
HAVING SUM(quantity) > 100;

children.summary: Joins combine rows from two or more tables based on a matching key, the SQL equivalent of an Excel VLOOKUP, but able to combine entire tables at once.

blocks.title: Types of Joins
rows: Only rows that match in both tables
All rows from the left table, matched where possible
All rows from the right table, matched where possible
All rows from both tables, matched where possible

blocks.content:
-- Try This
-- 1. List every order with the customer's name and order date.
-- 2. List customers who have never placed an order.


-- Answer
SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name, o.order_date
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

SELECT c.customer_name
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

children.summary: Beyond querying, SQL can also add, change, and remove data in a database using INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements.

blocks.title: Data Manipulation Statements
rows: Add new rows to a table
Change existing values in a table

blocks.content:
-- Try This
-- 1. Add a new customer, "K. Silva" from Kandy, joining today.
-- 2. Raise the price of product_id 5 to Rs. 620.
-- 3. Remove order_id 1042, which was cancelled.


-- Answer
INSERT INTO Customers (customer_name, city, join_date)
VALUES ('K. Silva', 'Kandy', CURRENT_DATE);

UPDATE Products
SET unit_price = 620
WHERE product_id = 5;

DELETE FROM Orders
WHERE order_id = 1042;

children.summary: Bringing SQL skills together to answer real business questions, such as finding top customers, monthly sales totals, or overdue invoices.

blocks.title: Practical Query Examples
items: Finding the top 10 customers by total revenue.
Calculating monthly sales totals broken down by region.
Listing all outstanding invoices past their due date.

blocks.content:
-- Try This
-- Find Ceylon Mart's top 5 customers by total amount spent, using
-- Orders, OrderItems, and Products.


-- Answer
SELECT
    c.customer_name,
    SUM(oi.quantity * p.unit_price) AS total_spent
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN OrderItems oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN Products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY c.customer_name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 5;

children.summary: SQL is powerful and near-universal for structured data, but it has limits worth knowing before relying on it for everything.

blocks.title: Benefits and Limitations
rows: Fast, even on very large structured datasets
Not designed for unstructured data like text or images
Supported by nearly every database system in use
Doesn't handle complex statistical modelling on its own
Precise and repeatable, the same query always returns the same result
Complex logic can become hard to read as queries grow

blocks.content: A quick reflection exercise: Ceylon Mart's manager asks you to predict next month's sales using SQL alone. Could you do it? SQL can easily give you the historical totals to work from, but predicting a future number is a job for the predictive analytics techniques from Module 2, often built in Python, not for SQL itself. Knowing where SQL's job ends is as useful as knowing SQL.

children.summary: Business Intelligence (BI) turns raw organizational data into dashboards and reports decision-makers can act on, typically supported by a dedicated BI team or function.

blocks.content: BI is less about a single tool and more about an organizational capability, combining data, technology, and people to consistently turn raw data into decisions. Larger organizations often have a dedicated BI team; smaller ones fold the responsibility into finance or operations.

Dashboards built without a process tend to turn into a pile of charts. The dashboard assignment in this course follows a 12-stage workflow, and the topics in this module each pick up a different part of it. Skim the whole list now so you know where you're heading.

blocks.title: The 12-Stage Dashboard Development Workflow
rows: Read the dataset description and review the column dictionary before building anything.
Identify the unit of observation, time period, dimensions, measures, categories, and limitations. Write a short data-understanding note.
Check row and column counts, data types, missing values, duplicates, date fields, unusual values, and major outliers. Record the issues you find.
Pick a realistic audience, such as utility management, customer service management, an economic analyst, a policy analyst, or a strategy team.
Write questions the dashboard should answer. They should be analytical, not simple lookups.
Choose the headline KPIs. For each one, state its definition and why it matters.
Use tables, charts, and summaries to look for trends, group differences, relationships, and anomalies before the final design.
Sketch a wireframe or layout first. Group related information and set a clear visual hierarchy.
Add meaningful filters or slicers, using time, geography, category, or other relevant dimensions.
Recalculate important numbers outside the dashboard. Test filters, totals, dates, labels, units, and blanks.
Write at least 3 key insights, and keep what you observed separate from what might explain it.
Submit the dashboard with its supporting documentation, and be ready to explain your design choices and findings.

children.summary: BI systems pull data from multiple source systems into one place before it can be visualized. This behind-the-scenes plumbing is the data pipeline.

blocks.content: A dashboard is only as good as the data feeding it. Before any chart can be built, data typically needs to be pulled from several source systems (sales, finance, HR), combined, and loaded somewhere it can be queried. That integration work is what a BI architecture is built to handle.

Stages 1 to 3 of the workflow all happen before you build anything. Read the dataset description and review the column dictionary first, then write a short data-understanding note and profile the data. Skip this and you end up summing the wrong field, or trusting a date column that's really just text.

blocks.title: What Goes in Your Data-Understanding Note (Stage 2)
items: Unit of observation: What one row actually represents, for example one order line, one customer, or one country in one year.
Time period: The dates the data covers.
Dimensions: The fields you can slice by, such as region, category, or customer type.
Measures: The numeric fields you add up or average, such as sales, kWh, or population.
Categories and limitations: The groups that exist in the data, and anything that limits what it can tell you.

blocks.title: Data Profiling Checks (Stage 3)
rows: Do they match the source and the column dictionary?
Are numbers stored as numbers and dates as dates, not text?
Which columns have blanks, and how many?
Repeated rows that would double-count your totals.
Valid dates, the full expected range, no strange formats.
Impossible values, or extreme ones that need investigating before you decide what to do with them.

blocks.content: Write down every issue you find. You'll need that list again when you validate the dashboard.

children.summary: KPIs are the specific, measurable metrics an organization tracks to judge whether it's meeting its goals, the numbers every BI dashboard is built around.

blocks.title: What Makes a Good KPI
items: Tied directly to a business objective, not just easy to measure.
Trackable consistently over time.
Owned by someone accountable for moving it in the right direction.

blocks.content: A dashboard should lead with 4 to 6 headline KPIs. Each one needs a clear label, a unit, and a written definition, plus a sentence on why it matters to the audience. If you can't explain why a KPI matters, it probably doesn't belong in the headline strip.

blocks.title: Documenting a KPI (Ceylon Mart Example)
rows: Quantity multiplied by unit price, summed across all order lines in the selected period
Shows the overall size of the business and whether it's growing
Number of distinct orders placed in the selected period
Shows how busy the stores are, separate from how much each order is worth
Total Sales divided by Order Count
Shows whether customers are spending more or less each time they buy
Customers with more than one order, divided by all customers who ordered in the period
A signal of loyalty, and cheaper growth than winning new customers

blocks.title: Get the Aggregation Right
items: Quantities can be summed: A total population can be added up across countries for one year, and so can sales or kWh.
Rates and percentages cannot: GDP growth, margins, and repeat-customer rates should never be summed across rows. Recalculate them from their parts, or use an average that actually makes sense.
Use consistent units: LKR, kWh, %, USD bn, people, years. Show the unit on every KPI.

children.text: Power BI Fundamentals & DAX Modeling Engine
children.summary: Power BI is Microsoft's business intelligence tool for building interactive dashboards, powered by DAX, its formula language for calculations.

blocks.content: Power BI connects to your data sources, lets you build a data model linking related tables together, and uses DAX (Data Analysis Expressions), a formula language similar in spirit to Excel formulas, to create calculated metrics that update automatically as new data flows in.

blocks.title: Build Filters That Earn Their Place (Stage 9)
items: Aim for at least 3 meaningful filters or slicers. If you use fewer, be ready to justify why.
Choose dimensions that suit the data, such as time, geography, or customer or economic category.
Every filter should change something meaningful. A slicer that moves no visual just confuses people.
After adding a filter, check that totals still agree across visuals and don't contradict each other.

blocks.title: Get the Data Model Ready
items: Dates as dates: Treat time fields as true dates or numbers. Stored as text, months sort alphabetically and April lands before January.
Document your measures: Write down what every calculated measure does and how it's worked out.

blocks.content: Here's what documented measures can look like for Ceylon Mart. Notice that Average Order Value is built from two other measures. It's recalculated from its parts, never summed across rows.

-- Total Sales (Rs.): quantity x unit price, summed over order lines
Total Sales = SUMX ( OrderItems, OrderItems[quantity] * RELATED ( Products[unit_price] ) )

-- Order Count: number of distinct orders
Order Count = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Orders[order_id] )

-- Average Order Value (Rs. per order): a ratio, so recalculate it from its parts
Average Order Value = DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], [Order Count] )

children.summary: The building blocks of an effective dashboard: the right chart types, layout, and interactivity, assembled to answer a business question at a glance.

blocks.content: A good dashboard is designed around the question the viewer needs answered, not around showing off every metric available. Layout, chart choice, and interactivity, like filters, matter just as much as the underlying data.
Start with the question, not the chart. Every major visual should have a purpose, and the number of visuals should stay manageable. More charts don't automatically mean better analysis.

blocks.title: What Every Dashboard in This Course Needs
items: One coherent dashboard experience. Multiple pages or tabs are fine where they make things clearer.
Headline KPIs with clear labels, units, and definitions.
Time-based analysis, where the dataset supports it.
Comparison across a meaningful category or segment.
Detailed visual that goes beyond a simple total.
Meaningful filters or slicers, unless you can justify using fewer.
Clear titles, axis labels, units, and legends where needed.
A visible source or data note, saying whether the dataset is synthetic or sourced from the World Bank.
A short insight section with the most important findings.
Consistent formatting, sensible number formats, and a readable layout.

blocks.title: Recommended Dashboard Structure
rows: Dashboard title, period selected, audience and purpose
Bar, column, heatmap, or map where appropriate
Scatter plot, decomposition, detailed table, distribution, or ranked view
Time, geography, customer type, region, category

blocks.content: Draw this layout as a wireframe before you open the tool (Stage 8). Group related information together and decide what the eye should see first.

children.summary: Once a report is built, it needs a plan for how it's shared with others and how often its underlying data refreshes to stay current.

blocks.content: A dashboard showing outdated numbers can be worse than no dashboard at all, because it still looks current even when it isn't. Publishing strategy covers who can see a report and where; refresh strategy covers how often its underlying data updates.

Validation (Stage 10) comes before anything gets shared. Recalculate important numbers outside the dashboard, and test the filters, totals, dates, labels, units, and blanks. Ask someone else to try it, or follow a structured self-test. Other people catch the problems you've stopped seeing.

blocks.title: Validation Checklist
items: The row count in the dashboard or data model matches the source dataset.
The date range matches the source dataset.
At least three key KPI values have been checked independently.
Filters change the visuals they should, and don't produce contradictory totals.
Totals and averages use appropriate aggregation.
Blank values have been handled on purpose, not by accident.
Currency, percentage, quantity, and date formats are correct.
Chart titles and units are accurate.
Top and bottom rankings have been checked for ties and missing values.
Every calculated metric is documented.
The dashboard has been tested by another person, or through a structured self-test.

blocks.title: What to Publish Alongside the Dashboard
items: Source note: Visible on the dashboard itself, including whether the data is synthetic or from a public source such as the World Bank.
Data-understanding note and profiling issues: What you found in Stages 2 and 3.
KPI definitions: What each KPI measures and why it matters.
Calculated metric documentation: How each custom measure is worked out.

children.summary: A report shows what the data says; a data story explains why it matters and what to do about it. Storytelling is what makes analysis actually change decisions.

blocks.content: It's entirely possible to build a technically perfect report that nobody acts on, simply because it presents numbers without a clear point. Data storytelling is the deliberate practice of shaping data into a narrative that leads a specific audience toward a specific decision.

On a dashboard, the storytelling lives in the insight section. The guidelines ask for a short set of the most important findings: at least 3 from your analysis, and usually no more than 8, each written as a concise finding with its implication.

blocks.title: What a Good Insight Section Does
items: Picks the findings that matter most, instead of listing everything the dashboard shows.
Says what each finding means for the audience, not just what the number is.
Keeps what you observed separate from what might explain it (more on that in Analytical Communication & Trend Exposure).

children.summary: Effective data storytelling combines three elements: accurate data, a clear narrative, and visuals that support, rather than distract from, the point.

blocks.content: Remove any one of the three and the story weakens. Data alone is dry and easy to misread, narrative without data is just opinion, and visuals without a clear point become decoration rather than communication.

children.summary: The same data needs different presentation depending on the audience. Executives typically want the headline and the decision; operational teams want the detail.

blocks.title: Adjusting for Your Audience
rows: The bottom line and a clear recommendation
One-page summary or a single headline chart
Enough detail to act on directly
Full dashboard or detailed data table

blocks.content: Choose a realistic audience before you design anything (Stage 4), and design for them, not only for yourself as the builder. What feels obvious to you can be invisible, or overwhelming, to someone who has never seen the data.

blocks.title: Realistic Audiences to Pick From
items: Utility management
Customer service management
An economic analyst
A policy analyst
A strategy team

blocks.title: Questions to Ask About Your Audience
items: Who will actually open this dashboard?
What decision will they make with it?
What do they already know about the data?
What can you leave out without hurting them?

children.summary: A well-structured data story follows a simple arc: set the context, state the problem the data reveals, then land on the insight or recommendation.

blocks.title: The Basic Arc
items: Context: What's the situation the audience needs to know?
Problem: What does the data show that's worth addressing?
Insight: What's the recommended takeaway or action?

blocks.content: Your analytical questions drive your story. They should move from description, through comparison, to interpretation. Avoid questions that only ask someone to read a value off a chart, because then the dashboard isn't adding any analytical value.

blocks.title: Seven Levels of Analytical Questions (Stage 5)
rows: What is the total or current level, and how has it changed over time?
Which customer types, regions, or countries differ most?
What trend is visible, and when do the major changes occur?
Is activity concentrated in a small number of segments?
Does one variable appear to move with another?
Which segments, periods, or entities behave unusually?
What should a manager investigate or monitor, based on the evidence?

blocks.content: One way to use the ladder: the first two levels set the context, levels 3 to 6 surface the problem, and the last level lands the insight and what to do about it.

children.summary: Clearly communicating a trend means showing not just the current number, but the direction and pace of change behind it.

blocks.content: A single number rarely tells the full story. "Revenue is $2M" means very little without knowing whether that's up or down, and by how much. Showing the trend behind a number is often more informative than the number itself.

blocks.title: Explore Before You Design (Stage 7)
items: Use tables, charts, and summaries to explore the data before settling on the final design.
Look for trends, differences between groups, relationships, and anomalies.
Include at least one time-based analysis where the dataset supports it.

blocks.content: Separating what you saw from why you think it happened is the hardest part of writing insights (Stage 11). An observation is something the data shows. An explanation is only a possibility. Don't make causal claims unless the data or the study design supports them.

blocks.title: Observation vs Explanation (Ceylon Mart Examples)
rows: Sales were higher in the months the promotion ran
Sales coincide with the promotion months
Colombo customers spend more per order
Average order value is higher among Colombo customers
Living in Colombo makes customers spend more
Beverage sales fell in the same period prices rose
The fall in beverage sales is associated with the price rise
The price rise killed beverage sales

blocks.title: Phrases That Fit the Evidence
items: "associated with"
"higher among"
"coincides with"

children.summary: Techniques that make a data story land: focusing on one central message, using comparison to add context, and cutting anything that doesn't support the point.

blocks.title: Techniques That Work
items: Lead with the takeaway, not the method used to get there.
Use comparisons and benchmarks to give a number meaning.
Cut anything, data or design, that doesn't serve the central point.

children.summary: Common mistakes that distort or confuse a data visualization, even when the underlying data is correct.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to Avoid
items: Truncated axes that exaggerate small differences.
Too many colours or categories crammed into one chart.
3D effects that distort how proportions are perceived.
Pie charts with too many slices to compare meaningfully.

blocks.title: Pitfall vs Better Practice
rows: Using a pie or donut chart because it looks attractive
Use it only with a small number of categories and a clear part-to-whole message. Otherwise prefer bars, lines, or scatter plots.
Keep the number of visuals manageable. More charts don't automatically mean better analysis.
Reserve strong, high-attention colours for exceptions, warnings, or selected states.
Show it, and explain it when it affects interpretation.
Use the correct aggregation. A population total can be summed across countries, but GDP growth cannot.
Use true dates or numbers, so months don't sort alphabetically.
Make filters understandable, and remove any that don't change a meaningful visual.
Causal claims the data can't support
Say "associated with", "higher among", or "coincides with" instead.
Use consistent units (LKR, kWh, %, USD bn, people, years) and label them.

children.summary: A framework for structuring an executive-level dashboard presentation so senior stakeholders get the decision-ready view they need.

blocks.content: Presenting to executives generally means leading with the recommendation first, then following with only the supporting evidence needed to justify it, the opposite order from how the analysis itself was actually built.

The seven-area layout from the BI module (header, KPI strip, trend, comparison, deep-dive, filters, insights) also works as a way to present. Open with the insights, since that's your recommendation, then walk through the evidence from the top of the dashboard down.

blocks.title: Before You Present
items: Draw a wireframe first, group related information, and set a clear visual hierarchy so the eye lands on the right thing.
Run through the validation checklist one more time.
Submit the dashboard together with its supporting documentation.
Be ready to explain your design choices and your findings.

blocks.title: Questions to Be Ready For
items: Why did you pick these KPIs?
Why this chart for this question?
How is this number calculated, and how do you know it's right?
What's missing from the data, and does it change the story?
Who is this dashboard for?

children.summary: Data can be stored in increasingly structured ways, from loose files, to databases, to purpose-built warehouses and lakes for large-scale analytics.

blocks.title: Storage Options
rows: Simple, small-scale storage, a single spreadsheet or document
Large volumes of structured data, optimized for analysis
Raw data of any type, structured or not, stored cheaply at scale

children.summary: Big Data is commonly described using five characteristics, the 5 V's, that set it apart from traditional, smaller datasets.

blocks.title: The 5 V's
items: Volume: The sheer amount of data generated.
Velocity: The speed at which it's generated and needs processing.
Variety: The different types and formats it comes in.
Veracity: How trustworthy and accurate the data is.
Value: The actual business usefulness gained from analyzing it.

children.text: Modern Data Architectures (ETL vs ELT Engine)
children.summary: ETL and ELT are two approaches to moving data into a system for analysis, differing in when the data gets transformed relative to when it's loaded.

blocks.title: ETL vs ELT
rows: Extract, then Transform, then Load (transformed before loading)
Extract, then Load, then Transform (transformed after loading)

children.summary: AI is increasingly built directly into data platforms, automating tasks like anomaly detection and report generation that once needed a human analyst.

blocks.content: Modern data platforms increasingly embed AI directly into the pipeline, automatically flagging unusual data, suggesting data quality fixes, or even drafting a first version of a report. That's shifting the analyst's role further toward review and judgement rather than manual production.

children.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are the technology behind tools like ChatGPT and Claude, trained on vast amounts of text to generate human-like responses and assist with analytical work.

blocks.content: An LLM is trained on enormous amounts of text and learns statistical patterns in language well enough to generate coherent, useful responses, including explanations, code, and drafted reports. For analysts, these tools are increasingly used as a "co-driver" for everyday tasks rather than a replacement for judgement.

children.summary: AI tools can now assist directly with everyday analytics tasks: cleaning messy data, drafting reports, and summarizing findings, speeding up work analysts previously did entirely by hand.

blocks.title: Where AI Assists Today
items: Automatically flagging inconsistent or suspicious data for review.
Drafting a first version of a written report or summary.
Summarizing a long dataset or document into key points.

children.summary: Prompt engineering is the skill of writing clear, specific instructions to an AI tool to get a useful, accurate response, increasingly a core analyst skill.

blocks.title: Habits of a Good Prompt
items: Be specific about exactly what you want and in what format.
Give the AI relevant context or data rather than assuming it knows your situation.
Ask it to show its reasoning or cite where information came from.

children.summary: AI tools can produce confident-sounding but incorrect answers, known as hallucinations. Responsible use means always verifying outputs before relying on them.

blocks.title: Responsible Practices
items: Independently verify any factual claim or number an AI tool produces before using it.
Disclose clearly when AI assisted with a deliverable.
Stay alert to bias that can be baked into AI-generated outputs.

children.summary: Data governance is the set of policies and responsibilities that keep an organization's data accurate, secure, and properly managed over time.

blocks.content: Without governance, data quality tends to degrade as an organization grows. Different teams define the same metric differently, and nobody is accountable for fixing errors. Governance assigns clear ownership (stewardship) and standards to prevent that.

children.summary: Data security protects information from unauthorized access, focusing on controlling exactly who can see or change which data.

blocks.content: Security is fundamentally about access control: making sure the right people can see and edit the right data, and that everyone else can't. This includes basics like password policies and permission settings, up through more advanced protections like encryption.

children.summary: Data privacy governs how personal information is collected, used, and eventually deleted, generally requiring an individual's informed consent.

blocks.content: Privacy is distinct from security. Security asks who can access data; privacy asks whether it's appropriate to collect and use that data about a person in the first place, and for how long it should be kept before being deleted.

children.summary: Governments worldwide have introduced data protection laws, GDPR in Europe and CCPA in California among the most influential, setting legal requirements for handling personal data.

blocks.title: Two Influential Regulations
rows: Broad individual rights over personal data, including the right to be forgotten
Consumer rights over the collection and sale of personal data

children.summary: Beyond legal compliance, data ethics asks whether using data in a particular way is fair, including whether an AI or algorithm might unintentionally discriminate against certain groups.

blocks.content: Something can be entirely legal and still be unethical. Algorithmic bias happens when a model, trained on historical data that reflects past inequalities, ends up making decisions that unfairly disadvantage certain groups, a risk that grows as more decisions get automated.
